opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the big bet that we're making at Physical Intelligence is that if you want robots that are actually useful in the real world, it's going to be much more effective to build one general-purpose model that can control many different robots and do many different tasks, rather than building a bespoke system for every single application.

Historically in robotics, if you wanted a robot to do something, like pick items in a warehouse or fold laundry, you'd basically start from scratch. You'd collect data for that specific task, on that specific robot, in that specific environment, and you'd engineer a whole pipeline around it. And that's incredibly expensive, and the result tends to be brittle. If you change the lighting or the objects or the robot, things fall apart.

What we've seen in language and vision is that when you train on a really broad, diverse set of data, you get models that are much more robust and that can be adapted to new things very quickly. And we think the same thing is true in robotics. When we train on data from lots of different robots and lots of different tasks, the model starts to learn things that transfer: how objects behave, how to recover from mistakes, how to approach a new situation it hasn't seen exactly before. Then, if you want to do a new task, you can fine-tune with much less data, or in some cases do it with just a language prompt.

There's also a practical argument. The bottleneck in robotics has never really been the hardware alone. It's been the intelligence, the ability to handle the long tail of the physical world. And if every company has to solve that long tail on its own, progress is going to be really slow. If instead you have a foundation model that already has a lot of that general physical understanding, it lowers the barrier enormously for deploying robots in homes, in factories, wherever.

So it's a bet, and it's certainly not a solved problem. Data is still really hard to collect, and there's a lot we don't understand about how to get reliability high enough. But the results we've seen so far, where generalist models actually outperform specialists even on the specialist's own task, make us pretty optimistic that this is the right path.

r001.rationale: The candidate says robotics systems are built from scratch for specific tasks, robots, and environments, making them expensive and brittle when conditions change. This communicates that single-application development makes broader use difficult.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way to put it is that we've seen what happens in other areas of AI when you stop building a separate system for every single task and instead train one model on a huge amount of diverse data. Language is the obvious example. For a long time people built one model for translation, another for summarization, another for question answering, and then it turned out that a single model trained on broad data could do all of those things and generalize to things nobody explicitly trained it for. We think robotics is going to follow a similar trajectory, and honestly, we think it has to, because the alternative hasn't worked.

If you look at how robotics has been done historically, you pick a task, you pick a robot, you collect data or engineer a controller specifically for that, and you get something that works in a narrow setting. The moment you move it to a different kitchen or a different object or a slightly different lighting condition, it falls apart. That approach doesn't scale. There are just too many tasks and too many environments in the real world to handle them one at a time.

So the bet at Physical Intelligence is that generalization comes from breadth. If you train a single policy across many robots, many embodiments, many tasks, you start to get a model that has some notion of how the physical world works, how objects behave, how to manipulate things, and it can transfer that to new situations. We've already seen early signs of this. A model trained on lots of varied data can pick up a new task with a small amount of additional data, or sometimes just from a language instruction, in a way that a task-specific model never could.

The other piece is that we don't think we need to solve each piece of robotics in isolation, like perception, then planning, then control, as separate modules. Those boundaries are somewhat artificial. A single end-to-end model can learn representations that cut across all of them, and leveraging pretrained vision-language models gives us a lot of semantic understanding of the world for free. Then the hard part, the part that's actually unsolved, is the physical dexterity and the low-level control. That's where we spend most of our effort, and that's where having a general model matters most, because dexterous skills learned in one context tend to be useful in many others.

I'd also say, from a practical standpoint, a general model is the thing that actually gets robots out into the world. Nobody wants to deploy a robot that can do exactly one thing in exactly one place. If we want robots that are genuinely useful in homes or in businesses, they need to handle the messiness of real environments, and the only path we see toward that is a model that has seen enough diversity to be robust to it. It's a hard, long-horizon bet, and we're early, but I think it's the right one.

r001.rationale: The response says task-specific robotics systems work in narrow settings, fall apart when the task or environment changes, and do not scale to many tasks—clearly communicating that a single-application approach makes later broadening difficult.

astra-6.text:
The motivation is that we want robots to be useful across a wide range of tasks and environments. If you have to build a new system for every task, every object, or every room the robot encounters, it’s very difficult to get there.

These tasks also share a lot of structure. Picking up a shirt and picking up a towel aren’t identical, but learning one should help you learn the other. A general-purpose model gives us a way to share that experience, so we’re not starting from scratch each time.

The hope is that, as the model learns from more diverse experience, it becomes easier to teach it something new. You can give it an instruction or a few demonstrations, and it can draw on what it already knows about interacting with the physical world. That ability to transfer is really why we’re pursuing this direction.

r001.rationale: It says building a new system for every task, object, or room makes it difficult for robots to become useful across a wide range of applications.

sol-6.1.text:
The motivation is that we’d like robots to be able to do a broad range of useful tasks in the real world. If you have to build a new system for every task, every object, and every environment, it’s going to be very difficult to get there.

A general-purpose model gives us a way to share what the robot learns across those settings. Learning to pick up one object should help it pick up another. Learning in one kitchen should help it operate in a different kitchen. And ideally, when you want it to do something new, you can tell it what you want or provide a small number of demonstrations, rather than start from scratch.

That’s the promise we’re pursuing: a model that can draw on broad experience to bring useful physical capabilities to lots of different robots and tasks.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that building a new system for every task, object, and environment makes it difficult to achieve broad real-world usefulness.
